lesson.title: por vs para
lesson.subtitle: Cause/exchange (por) vs goal/destination (para) — resolving the classic struggle

hook.title: Why English 'For' Hides Two Opposite Directions
hook.content: In English, 'for' points both forward toward a goal ('This gift is FOR you', 'I'm leaving FOR Madrid') and backward toward a cause or exchange ('Thanks FOR the invitation', 'I paid ten euros FOR the book'). Spanish separates those two mental pictures cleanly into para and por!

pattern.title: Para Is the Forward Arrow; Por Is the Cause, Scale & Path
pattern.content:
• **para** = the Forward Arrow →: recipient (un regalo para ti 'a gift for you'), destination (el tren para Madrid 'the train for Madrid'), deadline (para mañana 'for/by tomorrow'), and goal before an infinitive (para comprender 'in order to understand').
• **por** = the Cause, Scale & Path ⚖️: motive/cause (gracias por la invitación 'thanks because of the invitation', por favor), exchange/price on a scale (por diez euros), time of day (por la mañana), and path through space (por aquí 'this way / around here')!
pattern.linguist_note: Spanish por continues Latin prō + per; para fused Old Spanish por + a ('for-to' → forward direction).
pattern.trap_note: After prepositions (para, por, de, a, sin), 'yo' becomes mí (with an accent: para mí 'for me') and 'tú' becomes ti (without an accent: para ti 'for you')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: for (because of, in exchange for, through)

exercises.target_answer: para, por, un regalo para ti, gracias por la invitación, para comprender, por aquí
exercises.meaning: for (recipient, destination, deadline, 'in order to'), for (because of, in exchange for, through), a gift for you, thanks for (because of) the invitation, in order to understand, around here / this way
exercises.explanation: para points forward to the target/goal; por looks back at the cause, price, or path.

exercises.prompt: You bought a present to give to your mother (she is the recipient). Which preposition do you use?
options: Es un regalo por mi madre
Es un regalo para mi madre
Es un regalo a mi madre
exercises.target_answer: Es un regalo para mi madre
exercises.meaning: It is a gift for my mother
exercises.explanation: The recipient at the end of the forward arrow always takes para.

exercises.prompt: You are thanking someone BECAUSE OF their invitation. Which preposition follows gracias?
exercises.explanation: The invitation is the cause/motive of your gratitude (or what you give thanks in exchange for), so it always takes por: Gracias por...

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'It is a gift for tomorrow'
exercises.meaning: It is a gift for tomorrow
exercises.explanation: Deadlines and target dates point forward with para: para mañana.
Gracias por el café — gracias ALWAYS takes por!

diagnosis.cue: Gratitude looks back at the cause/reason, so gracias is always followed by por.

summary.outcome: Distinguish para (recipient, destination, deadline, 'in order to') from por (cause, exchange, path, time of day).

use_example.german: Gracias por el regalo — es para mi madre.
use_example.english: Thanks for the gift — it is for my mother.

summary.takeaway: para = forward arrow toward recipient, destination, deadline, or goal; por = cause, exchange, or path through.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1301] para: The Arrow): practice all four forward-arrow uses of para.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'It is for you (informal: para ti)'
twist.explanation: After a preposition like para or por, tú becomes ti: para ti!

foreshadow.line: Next in Topic 14: why Spanish possessives (mi/mis, su/sus) agree with the thing owned rather than the owner.

payoff.text: Because para came from por + a, it shares the exact same forward-pointing arrow feel as ir a from Topic 12!

para.english_meaning: for (recipient, destination, deadline), in order to
para.etymology_derivation: Old Spanish pora (por + a) — think of para as a forward arrow pointing at the recipient, destination, deadline, or goal ('in order to').

por.english_meaning: for (because of, in exchange for, duration), through, by
por.etymology_derivation: Latin prō + per — think of por as the cause behind an action, the price on a scale, or a path through space/time.

regalo.context_phrase: Es un regalo para mi madre.
regalo.context_translation: It is a gift for my mother.
regalo.etymology_derivation: English 'regale' comes from the same root.

invitación.etymology_derivation: Latin invītātiō. The -ción ending guarantees feminine gender: la invitación.

gracias.etymology_derivation: Latin grātia ('favor, grace'). Spanish thanks are plural: 'graces to you'.

mañana.context_translation: Tomorrow I am going to work.
mañana.etymology_derivation: As an adverb (mañana) it means 'tomorrow'; as a feminine noun (la mañana) it means 'the morning' (mañana por la mañana = 'tomorrow morning')!

mi.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the possession
mi.context_phrase: Es mi amigo y ellos son mis amigos.
mi.context_translation: He is my friend and they are my friends.
mi.etymology_derivation: Unstressed mi (no accent) means 'my'; accented mí (after a preposition: para mí) means 'me'!

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
